segments.text: (Reposted from Facebook, on January 17, 2017.) I am concerned about the number of people I've heard joking about Trump's election being evidence for the Simulation Hypothesis. Yes, I know it's a joke. I'm still concerned. Warning: #Essay, #LongEssay So as not to engage in Logical Fallacy: Appeal to Consequences, before I talk about why this joke is worrying, I shall first discuss why Trump's election does not in fact mean we are living in a simulation. And neither does the Berenstein/Berenstain Bears thing, etcetera. Because atheism generalizes. No, I'm not about to commit the Noncentral Fallacy (aka The Worst Argument In The World) by yelling "The Simulation Hypothesis is religious!" But once upon a decade, there was a time when lots of people believed in God. A time when atheism had to be argued, not just taken for granted. There was a time when believing in atheism made you one of those weird, loud people with arguments that only people with unusually good epistemology could follow, and other people talked about you exactly the way that the anti-LessWrong tumblrsphere now talks about LessWrong. Today, of course, atheism is just something that everyone in your filter bubble believes. But back then atheism had to be argued, and assessing the validity of those arguments required unusually good epistemology that left a lot of the audience behind, and other people laughed at those weird atheists and their snooty yet flawed epistemology on their primitive equivalents of Tumblr.

The Viking 1 probe operated on Mars's surface for six years, before its battery began to seriously degrade. It absolutely matters where ideas land and how they are applied, and when the existence of the entire human race is at stake, that’s no exception. If that’s obvious to you, this post is mostly just a collection of arguments for something you probably already realize. But if you somehow think technical AI safety or technical AI alignment is somehow intrinsically or inevitably helpful to humanity, this post is an attempt to change your mind. The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence.

This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs (Anthropic; OpenAI).

Reward hacking occurs when a reinforcement learning (RL) agent exploits flaws or ambiguities in the reward function to achieve high rewards, without genuinely learning or completing the intended task. Reward hacking exists because RL environments are often imperfect, and it is fundamentally challenging to accurately specify a reward function.

With the rise of language models generalizing to a broad spectrum of tasks and RLHF becomes a de facto method for alignment training, reward hacking in RL training of language models has become a critical practical challenge. Instances where the model learns to modify unit tests to pass coding tasks, or where responses contain biases that mimic a user’s preference, are pretty concerning and are likely one of the major blockers for real-world deployment of more autonomous use cases of AI models.

Hallucination in large language models usually refers to the model generating unfaithful, fabricated, inconsistent, or nonsensical content. As a term, hallucination has been somewhat generalized to cases when the model makes mistakes. Here, I would like to narrow down the problem of hallucination to cases where the model output is fabricated and not grounded by either the provided context or world knowledge.

There are two types of hallucination:

  1. In-context hallucination: The model output should be consistent with the source content in context.
  2. Extrinsic hallucination: The model output should be grounded by the pre-training dataset. However, given the size of the pre-training dataset, it is too expensive to retrieve and identify conflicts per generation. If we consider the pre-training data corpus as a proxy for world knowledge, we essentially try to ensure the model output is factual and verifiable by external world knowledge. Equally importantly, when the model does not know about a fact, it should say so.

This post focuses on extrinsic hallucination. To avoid hallucination, LLMs need to be (1) factual and (2) acknowledge not knowing the answer when applicable.

If you’re anything like me, you may have a lot of notes from various introspective activities – annual / monthly reviews, worksheets, therapy notes, etc. Often these notes are just gathering dust in a paper folder or some forgotten corner of Google Drive. There may be some insights there – how personal problems change over time, what things you tried and what worked and didn’t, and so on. One use case for capable AI models is to sift through this data and extract patterns, insights and interesting tidbits that you may have forgotten or not noticed. 

Here are some things I got AI to do for this analysis:

  • Transcribe handwritten worksheets and diagrams (I did have to take photos of the sheets – this was the most laborious part). The transcription was occasionally wrong and needed correction, but overall saved a lot of time. 
  • Summarize my answers to “Hamming questions” over the years. This was originally a CFAR worksheet named after Richard Hamming’s question “What are the most important problems in your field?” but applied to your life. 
  • In the past I have found it useful to make a visual representation of my problems as a graph showing how they contribute to each other. I had only a few of these from past years, so I asked AI to draw diagrams for each year based on my notes and worksheets.
  • Compare worksheets and diagrams from different years, identify persistent feedback loops, look how loops and key nodes change over time.
  • Identify interventions that worked in the past that I could try again (therapy and coaching notes are particularly good to mine for this). 
  • Do deep dives to analyze specific patterns. 

Claude Opus 5 and Fable did a pretty good job at this. Fable had a tendency to over-compress its findings, and I had to ask it to use simpler language. I also tried this 1-2 years ago, and I think the models are getting better at picking up non-obvious patterns.

Learnings about problems and patterns

Here are some patterns I found in my answers to Hamming questions over the past 10 years: 

  • Rate-limiting step / bottleneck: sleep, tiredness, focus, anxiety, and confidence were recurring themes over the past 10 years. On the one hand I made progress on these issues, and on the other hand they appeared from new sources, so overall there is some improvement but they are still there. 
  • Things I don’t feel “allowed to care about”: earlier years listed various things like having kids and mentoring others, which I eventually ended up doing. Creative pursuits also appeared on this list a lot (e.g. drawing or writing poetry) and I still don’t do much of this.
  • Things to do to “advance the plot” in my life: more regular meditation, try different kinds of therapy, getting help / advice sooner, more delegation / babysitting. 
  • Things I tend to do as a poor substitute for what I really need: general theme of procrastination and being reactive (scrolling social media, gravitating to logistical tasks over more open-ended tasks or hard decisions, joining projects run by others). Most of these have improved with better reflection and prioritization systems, but the core issues remain.
  • “My life is fine except X”: what came up as X has generally shifted from mostly mental problems (anxiety / overwhelm) to external / object level things (kids waking up at night, uncertain AI future etc). 

One thing I learned from this is that some of my persistent problems appeared in different guises or with different causes. These days I mostly attribute tiredness, lack of sleep and feeling overwhelmed to the demands of parenting, but looking back at my notes from 2015-17 this was just as much of an issue (if not more) before I had kids. There are internal and external factors affecting sleep, and the external factors have increased after having kids, but the internal factors are pretty stable and the same habits are still useful (e.g. put away screens and wind down after 10pm). 

Overwhelm was a recurring feeling triggered by different things (finishing my thesis, balancing research and outreach, taking care of a baby, etc) which seemed like a mental pattern that attached itself to life circumstances rather than a fact about those circumstances. I had a default response to having a lot of stuff going on with a sense of shame about not doing everything or comparing myself to others, and this made me feel overwhelmed (while the same circumstances did not feel as overwhelming when I gave myself permission to drop things). 

There were several persistent feedback loops between problems (which became weaker over time). 

  • The judgment loop: underperform → judge myself → feel anxious → perform worse. This comes up most clearly at work, but there is also a parenting version: feel anxious →  be triggered / impatient with kids → shame / guilt → anxiety. 
  • The pressure loop: feel behind → do lots of stuff compulsively → focus on small things and create more pressure → feel more behind. This has gotten better with explicit prioritization structures, but the compulsiveness pattern is still there, particularly when working on the computer (e.g. sometimes I find myself unnecessarily switching tabs). 
  • The disconnection loop: feel stressed → ignore internal signals → lose touch with what I want → more stress. This seems mostly fixed and didn’t show up in recent years. 

Comparing my bottleneck diagram from 2015 with one from 2025, there are some nodes in common (“should” mindset, confidence, anxiety) and some things that did not persist (neglecting internal signals, working memory, excessive effort, insomnia), which mostly map to solved problems. There are some new kid-related nodes though (“stress with kids” and “reduced alone time”). 

Learnings about approaches and solutions

There were various things that worked in the past that would be good to try again or do more often:

  • Reflection periods in a different physical location (library, park, coffee shop, etc).
  • Aiming for a crappy draft (to counteract writers block).
  • Noticing when I’m stuck with something and asking for help sooner. 
  • Aversion factoring: noticing if I’m avoiding doing something I would like to do, writing down what is good about doing it, what feels bad / aversive about it, and any counterpoints to those objections. I often ended up doing the thing after doing some aversion factoring on it. (Aversion factoring is traditionally taught with diagrams, but I found it easier to do in list form.)
  • Using anger / annoyance as an unblocker: noticing when I’m feeling stuck or tense and writing down what I feel annoyed about, which helps me to process emotions in the background and get into a more agentic mindset.

There were also things that I tried several times that didn’t work:

  • Putting time blocks on the calendar for things I intend to do, without supporting systems to make it happen. For example, reading blocks on my work calendar often got ignored in favour of project work that felt more urgent, and “alone time” calendar blocks on weekends kept not happening. If there are mental or situational obstacles to doing the thing, a calendar reminder is not sufficient. 
  • Closing comms channels (email / slack) to avoid distraction, e.g. during focus blocks. This didn’t alleviate the emotional reasons for getting distracted, and I often ended up going back to the comms channel to get some information I needed. What did work was to do focused work entirely on paper without a computer (reflecting in a notebook, reading a printed paper, etc). Deleting social media apps was also ineffective because I can open them in the browser (while using an app that prompts me to be intentional when I unlock the phone worked better).

I identified some meta-principles on things that tend to work for me:

  • Without chain of thought, I am not a general intelligence. I need to write everything down: todo items (before doing them), my mental state before starting work, thoughts about research directions or papers I read, loopy / obsessive thoughts, decisions, factoring aversions, etc. 
  • Habits that stick are usually attached to an existing routine: meditation after breakfast at work, leg stretches while using mouthwash before bed, doing regular exercise classes. One takeaway is that if I want creative pursuits to happen, I should sign up for a class in drawing or improv or something, and then I would actually do it. 
  • Habits that rely on willpower don’t work. It’s good to look for physical solutions to problems (medications / supplements, nasal spray for colds, weighted blankets, focused work in a different place without electronics, etc). Habits that necessarily have a mental component (like avoiding sugar / snacks) only work if I get into a mental frame where I just don’t do this thing, rather than a willpower-sapping frame of trying to do less of it.

Overall, the benefits I got from doing this kind of analysis can be broken down in two ways: looking at problems or approaches, and whether what I did was successful or not. I think each of these categories can be worth a deep dive with some AI help.

This is an annual post reviewing the last year and setting intentions for next year. I look over different life areas (work, health, parenting, effectiveness, etc) and analyze my life tracking data. Highlights include a minimal group house, the usefulness of Oura’s resilience metric, a small set of habits worth tracking, getting laser eye surgery, and Daniel starting school.

  1. 2025 review
    1. Life updates
    2. Work
    3. Health
    4. Parenting
    5. Effectiveness
    6. Travel
    7. Fun stuff
  2. Predictions
    1. 2025 prediction outcomes
    2. 2026 goals and predictions

2025 review

Life updates

  • We moved to a bigger house and a friend moved in with us. Not quite a group house, but a bit of community living and good company. It’s been fun and working well so far.
  • Daniel started school this year! We were very pleased to get our first choice of state school, which we were hoping to get into when we moved to this area. Daniel has been settling in well, and we have enjoyed the nice parent community and the 2-minute commute to the school.
  • I got laser eye surgery and I’m very happy with it, would recommend.

Work

Research

My research focus transitioned from dangerous capability evaluations to scheming propensity evaluations.

  • Paper: Evaluating Frontier Models for Stealth and Situational Awareness (blog post)
  • LASR scholars’ paper: Evaluating AI Agent Persuasion of Safety Monitors
  • Currently working on making honeypots for scheming models (also mentoring scholars working on this).

Outreach

  • Released a short course on AGI safety offering a concise and accessible intro to AI safety and governance (the Youtube playlist got 16K views so far).
  • Moderated a panel at the CHAI workshop constructing an argument map for AI risk.
  • Gave talks at EA Connect and GovAI.

Health

Physical health. This year I had 4 colds and one 3-day flu (probably mild due to the flu shot that I thankfully had this year). Dual defense spray doesn’t seem to be working as well as it used to, maybe because I haven’t been using it preventatively on a daily basis, which is probably less effective.

I’ve been getting more headaches than in previous years (8% of days, compared with 5% most years). Thursdays seem particularly bad, with twice the rate of headaches as other weekdays. It’s usually the day with the most meetings, so there is actually less screen time than other days. Maybe concentrating on people talking gives me headaches? Not sure what’s going on here.

I stopped eating processed sugar in late January, but the habit got gradually weaker from late summer. For some reason it feels less self-sustaining than it used to be. Maybe the difficulties with keeping the habit are mostly related to sleep deprivation (I didn’t manage it during the first year with either baby). Planning to get back on track this year.

I got laser eye surgery (SMILE) in May, and had a pretty quick recovery. The only persistent side effects were mild eye dryness that was treated with drops, and some halos around lights at night (which improved enough that I was comfortable driving at night a few months later). It’s pretty great to wake up in the morning and be able to see, not have to wear glasses if something goes wrong with my eyes, and not having to bring contact lens cases and solution everywhere. Overall this goes in the bucket of things I wish I had done years ago.

Mental health. Overall continuing the trend of significant improvement over 2021-23, returning to pre-kid baseline. There were 2 very bad mental episodes this year, same as last year. Travel seems to be less triggering than it was in the past.

Sleep (all metrics exclude jetlag days). Average sleep was 6.4 hours per night, similar to last year (6.3 hours). However, insomnia was higher at 18% of nights (compared to 13.5% in 2024). Misha had a sleep regression in the fall, and hours awake at night went up from ~1.1 to ~1.4. It seems to be generally higher early in the week and lower on weekends, not sure what that’s about (one hypothesis is office nights leading to disruptions).

Average sleep start time was 10 minutes after midnight (definitely room for improvement there). This seems to vary a lot by day of week, with Sundays much worse than other days (i.e. going to sleep half an hour later on Saturday evenings). I’m not sure why (but it seems relatively stable the last 2 years).

Oura has an overall “resilience” metric which I find useful, on a 1-5 scale (“limited” to “exceptional”), based on metrics of sleep quality, daytime stress and daytime recovery in the last 2 weeks. This seems to correlate pretty well with general wellbeing and productivity: “strong” (4) is peak performance, at “solid” (3) I feel well and make progress at work, at “adequate” (2) I’m sort of getting by / treading water, and at “limited” (1) I’m either ill or very sleep-deprived and should take sick leave. I spent most of 2024 at “adequate”, and things were looking generally good in 2025 until Misha’s sleep regression hit in September.


Parenting

It was an eventful year for Misha. He became very chatty and learned to climb everything climbable. At 13 months he started to sleep through the night, and at 20 months he forgot how to do that (the 2 year sleep regression strikes again). Sleep seems to be getting back on track though. We transitioned him out of diapers at 20 months, it was a slower process than with Daniel, but he got the hang of it eventually. Misha still gets along well with his brother, and much silly fun is had (unfortunately this sometimes ends with biting and crying, hope he will grow out of this soon).

I wrote more about the kids and my takes on parenting in this post.

Effectiveness

Habits. I stopped habit tracking in the Lights sheet a year ago, and some of my habits slipped (e.g. bedtime and using the defense spray daily). At the time I was tracking 16 habits, which was way overkill and had high overhead. I am going back to doing habit tracking (in my life tracking spreadsheet for simplicity) for the following habits:

  • meditation
  • acceptance / negative visualization practice
  • use defense spray
  • go to bed by 11

Time tracking. Some increase in research+reading time in the H2 2025 relative to H1 2025 or H2 2024. Work hours have recovered from the post-parental-leave slump in 2024.


Deep work. This measures average deep work hours per day on workdays. I previously observed some correlation between Deep work and the resilience metric, and the graphs mostly have the same peaks (except June, which was unusual due to travel and conferences).


Digital habits. The number of times I open my phone per day has been increasing over the last 3 years (average of 27 in 2023, 32 in 2024, 37 in 2025). I used to use the Intenty app that asked me why I’m opening my phone, but they made some annoying changes to the app and I stopped using it. Looks like it’s been updated again, so I’ll give it another go. I still use grayscale by default, which helps.


External engagements. I track various external engagements I get invited to do, and how much I regret doing them. Most requests are outreach-related (speaking, reviewing, organizing) and some are research-related (research talks and mentorship). The table shows numbers for all requests (with numbers for outreach requests in brackets). Overall there is more regret for outreach engagements, but this year both regret rates are at all-time low. Hopefully I’m developing a better sense for which commitments are worthwhile.

Travel

We went to Slovenia for some hiking and sightseeing. I had been there once before for the 2006 IMO, so it was a nostalgic trip for me. A few places felt familiar, but otherwise it was like visiting a new country. We had a 2-day hiking trip between huts, and Daniel hiked 10km on both days (though not without some complaining).

When we visited Toronto over Christmas, Daniel was excited to learn cross-country skiing. We got him some used skis and boots from a second hand sports shop, which gradually fell apart over the course of the week. Thankfully the weather gods graced us with enough snow to practice in the local park, and Daniel was getting the hang of it by the end.

We visited Janos’ sister and family in Florida over New Year’s, it was my first time there. It was unseasonably chilly, but we still got a couple of days on the beach. Misha tried to run into any body of water he could see (including the ocean) so we had to keep an eye on him (he was much more interested in the lake than in posing for a sunset photo).

Fun stuff

  • Books: Wabi Sabi, 123 Magic, Feeding your demons, Weirdest people in the world, If anyone builds it everyone dies.
  • I’ve been hosting more parties and EA parents meetups since we moved to a house with a big living room.
  • Janos and I did an unofficial tour of London saunas and visited at least 7. I particularly liked the community saunas, they have outdoor wooden sauna rooms with some nature outside.
  • I learned how to propagate a plant, by putting a branch into water to grow roots. It actually grew this big in a few months! (The one on the left was a branch that Misha broke off the one on the right, and I had to make it into a new plant.)

This post is a collection of parenting takes that sometimes go through my head, based on my experience raising our two boys (5 and 2 years old). All of this is based on my experience and might not apply to others (see the law of equal and opposite advice).

  1. Potty training
  2. School can be good actually
  3. Mental health
  4. Travel with kids
  5. Birth
  6. Miscellaneous

My overall parenting philosophy is pretty hands off with a focus on learning key skills early (potty training, reading, numeracy). We try to give the kids lots of free play and opportunities to do what they want, while encouraging independence and helpfulness. 

Potty training

We followed roughly the same process for both kids – a few months of “pre-training” for regularly using the potty, and then transitioning out of diapers with the “oh crap” method, at 18 months for Daniel and 20 months for Misha. The overall philosophy was similar to how my grandfather trained me when I was a baby – start early, lots of practice and repetition. 

I think it was helpful to get them used to using the potty from an early age and establishing a potty routine at times when they were likely to go anyway (after naps and meals). Transition out of diapers at an early age seemed easier this way – it was a smaller step from “use the potty at these points of the day” to “use the potty every time you need to go”, rather than a “zero to hero” transition for a child who’s never used a potty before. The pre-training period also provides a much better signal for readiness to potty train than we would otherwise have (things like “interest in the toilet” are too noisy to be a reliable signal). 

I’ve seen some concerns about confusing the child by using the potty while still wearing diapers, but I have not found this to be a problem for my kids. Maybe this is more of an issue for training older kids, I think 1-year-olds are not really aware enough to pick up on this and be confused by it. 

The process was easier with Daniel than with Misha, maybe because I did more pre-training with Daniel and generally invested more effort. The active transition was about 3 days with Daniel and about 2 weeks with Misha, with 1-2 accidents a day for a few months afterwards. What definitely made it easier in both cases is that the kid was with a nanny rather than in nursery, and the nanny helped a lot with the potty routine and the training process. 

School can be good actually

There seems to be a common view in rationalist-adjacent circles that schools are bad and waste all the kids’ time and you should homeschool your kids instead. (This is largely coming from the US, where the education system seems particularly bad, and I think does not apply as much to other parts of the world.) I directionally agree with this perspective that it’s important to consider whether your kids are actually learning in school and how well they are spending their time, and I think this should be an important factor in your choice of school and other possible alternatives. 

Based on our research and tours of ~20 primary schools in London, schools vary a great deal in their educational philosophy, atmosphere, and level of structure. There are good schools where kids are happy and actually learning things. Other parents are also looking for this, so good schools tend to be massively oversubscribed for a reason (I think this is a more reliable indicator of school goodness than official school ratings, though of course these are correlated). There is a lot of available data about different aspects of school quality, including parent surveys about how happy and safe kids feel there, and of course academic performance scores, and schools vary a great deal on these dimensions. 

In my childhood, both the worst times and the best times were at (different) schools. I was bullied in middle school and had a pretty bad time. Then I transferred to a STEM-focused school attached to the Kyiv polytechnic university, where I learned a lot and found a great community of nerdy kids who loved math. That was a formative experience for me, and I kept looking for the same nerd community vibe after my family immigrated to the West, in Canadian high school math camps and eventually in the rationalist community. Great schools definitely exist, you just have to find them. 

Mental health

The impact of becoming a parent on mental health seems complicated and probably varies a great deal between people. I think it depends a lot on your baseline – if you have existing issues with depression / anxiety / perfectionism, these can get worse from being triggered more often and exacerbated by sleep deprivation. At the same time, kids are often a great source of happiness and meaning. The overall effect seems hard to predict, but worth being prepared for mental health challenges or changes in the early years. 

My mental health got worse in the first few years after becoming a parent, though it’s hard to disentangle various depressing confounders around this time (the pandemic, my father’s death, the invasion of Ukraine). There were particular ways that parenting seemed to interact with my mental health issues. I had chronic anxiety before, which was slowly getting better with therapy / circling / meditation, but having a kid gave me so much more to be anxious about. I sometimes had difficulties liking myself and accepting when I made mistakes, and the generator of this got a lot of ammunition when I was taking care of a baby and made a lot of mistakes (defined fairly broadly as “something went wrong and I could have conceivably prevented it”). I hoped that the sheer amount of “exposure therapy” would teach me to be kind to myself, but this didn’t happen on its own and required some sustained effort. 

At the same time, being a parent provided more motivation to overcome mental health problems by raising the stakes. I could observe how not taking care of myself directly translated into negative impact on my kids when I was more anxious and impatient around them and set a bad example for them if I was yelling or freaking out. I got a more visceral sense that self-care is not indulgence or laziness but a necessary component of being a good parent. I feel like I have resolved some longstanding mental issues that would be more difficult to fix if I didn’t have this incentive.

Timing-wise, having kids in my early thirties was a good balance between having time to work on my career and mental health in my twenties, and still having the biological ability and energy to have kids and take care of them. Having kids 3 years apart also worked pretty well, it was definitely less overwhelming to take care of one small child at a time (and contrary to some worries I had, the age gap was not an impediment to playing together). 

Travel with kids

We travel with the kids a fair bit (usually to nature destinations or to see family). Most trips have some accompanying childcare (usually traveling with a grandparent, and once we stayed in a hotel with a kids club where we could leave the kids until 6pm). A trip with kids without childcare is not vacation. Taking care of young children all day in an unfamiliar environment is exhausting and I would not recommend it. 

I have found that staying in one place during the trip makes things a lot easier than moving around (because you have a lot of stuff to pack and unpack). An apartment with a kitchen is much better than a hotel room – you can make and store food for the kids and have enough space. It’s generally good to have the option to cook at the accommodation, since going out to restaurants with little kids can be tricky and stressful (my toddler loves to run off and get into the staff-only areas). It’s good to have flexible plans and different options for activities depending on what the kids (and the parents) are up for at that time. 

Birth 

I would describe myself as a sort of “pragmatic naturalist” when it comes to birth philosophy. I generally felt like my body knows how to do this birth thing and I just need to get out of the way, while also accepting interventions when they make sense (e.g. we planned a home birth for Misha, but ended up inducing him in hospital at 42 weeks). 

I didn’t use medical pain relief, because it was easier to deliver the baby standing up and being able to feel their position (also I find the idea of a needle in my spine really creepy). I think physical pain during birth can be traumatic or epic, depending on your perceived level of agency and how supported you feel. I was fortunate to have the support of a wonderful doula (and of course my husband) both times, and I got through it with chanting and heat packs. Of course, I was very lucky to have uncomplicated births – if medical intervention is needed, that’s a very different situation. 

People have widely different preferences on birth, and having your wishes respected and honored is a big factor in having a positive experience. I highly recommend writing down a “birth plan” detailing your preferences and contingency plans, and having someone with you to advocate for them during birth (this is something doulas are great at). 

Miscellaneous

Childcare. We are very fortunate to have a nanny, who makes our life much easier. It’s a big load off not to deal with dropoffs and pickups and the barrage of germs that comes with nursery, and the nanny helps with some housekeeping and does baths and dinner for the kids. If you have multiple children, it can be cheaper to hire a nanny than to pay for several nursery places. Nursery is good for socialization (starting ~2 years of age) and connecting with other local parents, so we might send Misha to nursery sometime next year.

Screen time. We usually don’t let them interact with phones, and watch some things on the TV together (e.g. Magic School Bus and Bluey are big favorites). We sometimes used youtube videos to motivate toddlers to do things like getting dressed and toothbrushing, or to calm them down from a tantrum.

Discipline. We use timeouts sparingly, usually counting is enough and actually doing a timeout is pretty rare. We found that timeouts are more effective for stopping naughty behavior and less effective for misbehavior driven by upset / anger (where they don’t have enough self control, and giving them space usually works better). 

Food. We have a pretty hands off approach to food, we just offer a bunch of things and don’t make them eat things they don’t want to. They cycle through different phases where sometimes they are really into vegetables and sometimes they want only pasta, which seems fine. 

Sleep. We have a pretty late bedtime for our kids (9:30-10pm). This allows us to spend more time with them in the evening and go to evening events (e.g. visiting friends). The toddler wakes up at 7:30am, and the 5 year old needs to be woken around 8am for school. We sleep trained both of them around 1 year of age, which mostly consisted of stopping nursing at night. Both kids had a sleep regression shortly before the second birthday, which seemed to have resolved for Misha when we put him to sleep with his brother.

Reading. We taught Daniel to read at around 3.5-4 years of age, using flashcards, spelling games and phonics books (highly recommend Julia Donaldson’s phonics series). It got easier once he started blending letters into words, and he’s enjoyed being able to entertain himself by reading simple books on his own. 

Motivation. We’ve found it effective to use rewards with Daniel. We have chocolate treats for good boys who get out of bed, get dressed for school, help with the laundry / dishwasher, etc. This seems pretty motivating for him, even as an abstract concept (he sometimes forgets to get the actual treat at the end). We haven’t tried more complicated things like sticker charts yet, that sounds helpful for older ages.

Systems. We have set up some systems for distributing parenting labour (without this, it’s easy to fall into a pattern of me doing things by default). We have 3 “office nights” per week, when one person has a free evening (used for work or personal time) and the other takes care of the kids. When our kids woke up early in the morning (around 6-18 months), we had an alternating schedule for morning duty (neither of us is a morning person). We also have a planning sync meeting once a week to batch various parenting logistics and decisions. 

Favorite parenting books:

  • How to Talk so Little Kids Will Listen
  • Hunt Gather Parent
  • Siblings Without Rivalry
  • Oh Crap! Potty Training
  • 123 Magic 
  • Positive Birth Book

These are some things that have worked for us in our parenting journey so far. I hope some of these takeaways will be interesting or useful to others.

I’ve been doing life tracking for around 10 years, and this post is looking back at some things I learned from the data (since my previous retrospective in 2017). Highlights include what I get out of the Oura ring, correlations between sleep and deep work / distraction, seasonal patterns in health, and regret patterns for external commitments. I also review various productivity / effectiveness systems I have tried and which ones have stuck around after 10 years. I analyze this data annually in my new year review posts, and this post will look at longer-term trends.

These are the main types of tracking that I do:

  • Oura ring automatically tracks sleep data (timings, night wakings, heart rate at night, etc)
  • Spreadsheet for recording other metrics manually (insomnia, meditation, exercise, illness, number of times I unlocked my phone, etc)
  • Work stuff: time tracking, deep work hours, and recording external engagements

My usual process is: export metrics from Oura, add them to the life tracking sheet, then visualize and analyze the data using python scripts (which I’m happy to share).

Correlations. Looking at correlations between different metrics (with a disclaimer that there are many possible confounders and causality is often unclear). Unsurprisingly, the strongest correlations are between various sleep metrics (for the preceding night). Most things are not correlated, but a few things stand out.

  • It’s interesting to see distinct effects from “insomnia” (binary variable, 1 if I was unable to sleep for over an hour at night) vs “hours awake at night” (awake time in bed recorded by Oura). Hours awake at night are usually caused either by insomnia or taking care of kids at night. “Lowest resting heart rate” (a metric of poor sleep quality) is positively correlated with “insomnia” but not with “hours awake at night”. “Hours awake at night” has some negative correlation with “deep work hours”, but this is almost zero for “insomnia”. One hypothesis is that being woken up by kids makes me tired while insomnia doesn’t, which leads to deeper sleep when I go back to sleep (hence the lower heart rate) and worse work output the next day.
  • Health variables (respiratory symptoms and headaches) don’t seem to be correlated with anything else. Too bad, I was hoping there would be a clue for the cause of headaches in here.
  • “Meditation mean” (proportion of past 4 days when I meditated) has some correlation with less night waking, more deep work, and checking my phone less (which is a measure of distractability).
  • “Exercise mean” (proportion of past 4 days when I exercised) is correlated to going to sleep earlier, but also correlated with “hours awake at night” – not sure what this is about.
  • “Phone unlocks” is correlated with fewer hours of sleep and waking up late, interesting that there is no correlation with “deep work hours”.
  • “Deep work hours” is correlated with the Oura “resilience to stress” metric, which is on a 1-5 scale (“limited” to “exceptional”). I’ve experienced the 1-4 range on this metric and never reached a 5. Days with “resilience” 3-4 (“solid-strong”) have around 50% more deep work hours than days with “resilience” 1-2 (“limited-adequate”).

Sleep. Looking over my sleep patterns over the years (as usual, excluding jetlag days). There were substantial changes after having children (born in late 2020 and late 2023): decreasing hours of sleep (from ~7 hours to ~6.3 hours per night), a lot more hours awake at night, and much earlier bedtime (from ~1:30am in 2017 to ~11:30pm now). Insomnia decreased after doing a sleep restriction program in 2017, then increased when each child was born and went down again to the 2018-19 baseline.

The Oura ring has been pretty useful for automatically tracking these metrics. It also seems to have a good holistic picture of how I’m doing, e.g. it usually predicts when I’m getting sick a couple of days ahead of clear symptoms.

Weekly and annual patterns. There were patterns in some of the metrics over days of the week or time of year.

  • Deep work hours (time spent on focused research activities, such as reflection or reading, but not e.g. running experiments or debugging). These were highest on Thursdays and Fridays – maybe because my focus tends to ramp up as the week progresses, or maybe because Thu / Fri were no-meeting days at different points.
  • Deep work hours were higher in summer and lower in winter. This might suggest lower output during darker months of the year (though October & November seem more productive than the spring, which contradicts this).
  • Respiratory symptoms have some seasonal patterns, worst in October and November (start of the flu season) and for some reason July. I had basically no respiratory illness in 2020 (due to to covid lockdowns) and a peak in 2022 when Daniel started at nursery (it looks like I was sick about a quarter of days – this was before I found the defense spray for colds).
  • Headaches also have seasonal patterns, worst in summer and with a significant peak in July – what is up with July? Some hypotheses include dehydration and pollen. I didn’t previously consider myself to have pollen sensitivity, but given this headache graph, maybe I should…

Work time tracking. I track time during work hours (10am – 6pm on weekdays) and also if I do work outside those hours (e.g. weekend conferences). There is some variation in total work hours, correlated with the age of youngest child (the hours bounced back faster after the second kid, probably due to having a private nanny looking after both kids at home). I mostly try to get the research + reading time to go up, and tracking this has been helpful for creating the space for this (e.g. booking enough focus time blocks).

External commitments. I’ve been tracking various external engagements I get invited to do, and how much I regret doing them. I found that I tend to regret reviewing papers and organizing the most, and this gave me motivation to decline almost all conference reviewing requests going forward (on the other hand, maybe I should give more research talks).

Systems. I’ve tried various systems over the years, with an overall trend towards simplifying and reducing overhead, and the systems that provide the most benefit for the amount of overhead have stuck around.

Systems I consistently used in the last 5-10 years:

  • Life tracking sheet (I no longer fill out a form daily, just update the sheet every few days)
  • Workflowy for todos and notes
  • Google docs for logging, journaling and reflection
  • High-level time tracking for work
  • Work cycles (on and off)
  • FollowUpThen
  • Weekly & monthly review process
  • Form for evaluating external engagement requests

Systems I used for years but no longer use:

  • Intend / Complice (6 years). A bit too much overhead (e.g. categorizing intentions into goals). I didn’t like committing to intentions and not being able to change them.
  • Lights spreadsheet for habits (4 years). This was somewhat useful for establishing habits and reminding myself of my intentions. It was tedious to fill out every day and I often ended up with a backlog. I found that the main factor in consistently doing a habit was having specific times / triggers for it during the day (e.g. meditation after breakfast), and tracking it on the Lights sheet didn’t add significant benefit over that.

Systems I tried and dropped quickly:

  • Goal tracking (Beeminder, 42goals)
  • Detailed time tracking with Toggl (work & personal time).

Overall this was a pretty good year. Highlights include adjusting to life with two kids, moving out of the group house, lots of travels, and camping with kids for the first time.

2024 review

Life updates

We moved out of the group house and got our own place near a school we like. We miss it a lot, but it’s also nice to have our own space. We are enjoying the new neighbourhood (walking distance from 5 different parks and still a bike commute from the office).

Work

I spent the first half of the year on parental leave and the second half working – often tired and not super focused, but still happy to be back. I found that tiredness does not have a uniform effect on my thinking / focus abilities, but more of a “dropout effect”, where some proportion of thoughts become incoherent, and more gaps in attention than usual. 

Research

  • Our paper on dangerous capability evaluations came out in March! 
  • Continuing in this line of work, focusing on deceptive alignment capabilities.

Outreach

  • Updated the Paradigms in AI alignment talk and gave the talk at the Alan Turing Institute and the Women in AI safety meetup. 
  • Took part in a panel on Current issues in AI safety at the Vienna alignment workshop.
  • Major updates to our internal AI alignment course.

Health

Physical health

Overall pretty good. I had 5 short mild colds, and one normal cold (when I ran out of defense spray). Looking at the number of days I had cold symptoms (including mild ones), there has been a declining trend since 2022 (when I had a cold 12% of the time).

I was intending to get back to avoiding processed sugar this year, but didn’t manage this. I also dropped the habit the first year after Daniel was born, so maybe this is generally hard to keep up when caring for a baby (with intensive breastfeeding and spending more time at home). Will try to get back into it this year.

Mental health

  • Overall a lot less anxiety with the second baby. Had only two night terrors last year, basically not an issue. 
  • Only two episodes of very bad mental states early in the year. Feels like this might be a permanent shift, a bit early to tell though.
  • Last year I observed that bad mental states are mostly triggered by travel, and I was expecting we would be doing less travel. We still ended up traveling a lot, but I found it less stressful once we got used to the dynamics of handling two kids. I still felt overwhelmed at times, especially when camping, but I had more mental capacity to cope with it.

Sleep. Comparing the sleep metrics this year to the first year with Daniel, the amount of sleep is pretty similar (average 6.3 hours a night), but there was a lot less insomnia in the first half of the year with Misha. (As usual, all the sleep metrics are excluding jetlag.)

Parenting 

Newborn period. Was easier this time than with Daniel. Breastfeeding was simpler and Misha got the hang of it faster. Night wakings were shorter than with Daniel (around 20 minutes vs 1 hour), partly because I was more easy-going about cosleeping. 

Grandparents. My mom and Janos’s dad came again to stay with us for a few months each. My mom took care of Daniel and made lots of food. Janos’s dad took Misha to the park for long naps, so I had a few hours to myself in the middle of the day. This made the newborn period a lot easier and we are very grateful for their help.

Sleep. Misha took a while to sleep for longer stretches at night, and he is still not sleeping through the night. We sleep trained Daniel around 9 months, but haven’t managed this with Misha. It’s been harder to get him to wean off night feedings, since he tends to persistently cry until he’s fed, but he seems to be gradually learning how to settle himself.

Comparing the number of night feeds and awake hours in the first year with Daniel vs Misha, I see that night feeds were much lower for Daniel at the end, but awake hours were only slightly lower. Night feeds only count feeds between 12 and 6am, while hours awake (exported from Oura) counts any awake time between going to sleep and waking up. So I think one-year-old Daniel was sleeping through until the early morning, then I woke up to feed him, and went back to sleep (if I wasn’t doing the morning shift).

Returning to work. I went back to work when Misha was 6 months old, and Janos was on leave with him for the summer. He had some challenges with feeding Misha at first, because he refused to drink from a bottle, and only ate from a spoon (which was a bit slow). Misha ate some solids while I was at work, and was always eager to feed when I came home. In retrospect, I probably returned to work too early, because I was too tired to make meaningful progress.

Misha’s potty use. Similar pattern to Daniel so far. Misha often did #2 on the newborn potty, which was pretty convenient. This lasted until 5 months when he started solids and outgrew the potty. He’s been gradually getting used to the regular potty from around 9 months, though he is often restless and mostly uses it to practice standing up.

Daniel’s night training. Continued on a good trajectory, and didn’t get worse when Misha was born (as sometimes happens to older siblings). There was a cluster of accidents in March for some reason, and grandpa retrained him. Overall there were 15 night accidents this year until they stopped at the end of summer, so Daniel was completely dry by his 4th birthday!

Sibling dynamics. The time when Misha became mobile and started crawling around was challenging for Daniel, and he often tried to control what Misha is doing and take away his toys, especially if he was in a bad mood. He generally tends to be bossy, and now there was someone he feels he can be in charge of! Misha can retaliate by biting and pulling Daniel’s hair, so things can escalate quickly. The amount of conflict seems to be decreasing and the kids are getting along pretty well. We still need to watch out even when they are playing together happily, because Daniel is big and energetic and likes to play rough, so things can go quickly from laughing to crying. Overall they seem to like each other a lot and it’s really sweet :). 

Relationship effects. With two kids, Janos and I have less time with each other by default. We have a weekly babysitting time on Sundays that we use to have our check-in and date night. This has been very helpful for staying connected and cooperating with each other.

Effectiveness

Lights habit tracking. I stopped using the Lights spreadsheet in November because it was too much overhead. I often didn’t fill them in for days and then had a backlog, so it turned into more of a habit tracking mechanism than a reminder to actually do the habits. It seems like the main factor in following through on a habit is whether there is a regular time and context for doing it (e.g. doing stretches after brushing my teeth in the evening) and how much it is disrupted by travel (e.g. I usually meditate after breakfast on workdays, but this often doesn’t work when traveling). If I have this regular time, then I don’t really need to check off the habit in a sheet to do it consistently. 

Time tracking. This year, in an average work week, I spent a similar amount of time on research, reading, and outreach, and a lot less time in meetings than last year.

This year, I spent 25 hours on work activities (compared to 30 last year). I often started work later in the day due to parenting responsibilities and logistics (and did not reliably track this, so the “total non-work” number is an underestimate. It was harder to get enough work hours in when Janos was on leave in summer, and easier in the fall when we got a nanny. I also started doing an office night once a week late in the year when Misha was older and it was easier for others to put him to bed.

Managing logistics. There were a lot more logistics with two kids. Janos and I started doing a weekly “planning sync” meeting where we coordinate on logistics, planning and decisions. This takes up time during work hours, but probably saves time overall by batching these tasks and communicating more efficiently.

Digital habits. Phone unlocks (number of times I unlock my phone per day) went up this year compared to last year. I didn’t use grayscale on my phone as much, and stopped using the Intenty app in the summer (the app had an update that made it more annoying). The number of unlocks went up, but is still in a reasonable range of around 30-35 a day.

External engagements. The number of external requests (speaking, reviewing, etc) went back down to a manageable level this year (I assume the parental leave autoresponder played a role). The regret rate (0-1) was similar to previous years at 0.19.

Looking at regret stats for 2017-2024, the engagements I regret the most tend to be reviewing and organizing. It seems like the average quality of assigned papers has gone down in recent years, so I endorse doing little or no reviewing going forward (and I hope the task of filtering out bad papers will be automated by AI soon).

Travel 

We traveled quite a lot this year! With grandparents around and a lot of parental leave this year, it was an opportune time to travel. We visited France, Hungary, Netherlands, Canada, Morocco, and a few places in the UK.

Our first trip with little Misha was to Snowdonia in north Wales. I couldn’t do much walking uphill while carrying a 6kg baby, but we had a good time hiking around a mountain lake (Daniel walked most of it).

We went to Burning Nest (a local Burning Man event in the UK). This was our first time camping with the kids. We were a bit underprepared in terms of gear – next time we would bring warmer sleeping bags (the nights were surprisingly cold for late May), get a big family tent instead of using two regular tents, and a canopy for the kitchen area. Our camp wasn’t a great place to be when it rained, so we ended up hanging out a lot in theme camps (which were very nice and welcoming). With kids in tow, we didn’t manage to go to any scheduled events, so we were exercising our spontaneity wandering around and bumping into interesting things.

In summer we went to a friend’s birthday weekend in the Netherlands, and we decided to make it a road trip using the ferry across the English channel. It was a bit longer than going by plane, but also more relaxing (the ferry had a cafe and a kids playground, so it was a great break from driving). The kids did pretty well with spending a day in the car and slept a lot.

We’ve been meaning to return to the Canadian Rockies, and finally made it happen this year. With two kids in tow, this was pretty different from our first trip in 2006, which was all about climbing summits. This time we did relatively flat trails around cirques and lakes, within range of what Daniel could walk by himself (~5-6km with ~200m elevation), with some intermissions where Janos carried him and I carried Misha (who was 10kg at that time).

We usually go to Canada over Christmas, but this time we’re going there later in the winter, so we decided to spend Christmas on our own somewhere warm and sunny. We spent a week in Morocco (our first visit to Africa), staying in a big hotel with babysitting (so we had some time to ourselves). We did a few outings to visit the medina in Marrakech (very interesting but a bit stressful with kids), ride camels, and take a quick look at the Atlas mountains (with some experience of chaotic local driving). Mostly we were chilling at the hotel, enjoying the wonderful Moroccan hospitality and stocking up on sunshine to take back to London in our hearts.

After 7 years at Deep End (and 4 more years in other group houses before that), Janos and I have moved out to live near a school we like and some lovely parks. The life change is bittersweet – we will miss living with our friends, but also look forward to a logistically simpler life with our kids. Looking back, here are some thoughts on what worked and didn’t work well about living in a group house with kids.

Pros. There were many things that we enjoyed about living at Deep End, and for a long time I couldn’t imagine ever wanting to leave. We had a low-effort social life – it was great to have spontaneous conversations with friends without arranging to meet up. This was especially convenient for us as new parents, when it was harder to make plans and get out of the house, particularly when we were on parental leave. The house community also made a huge difference to our wellbeing during the pandemic, because we had a household bubble that wasn’t just us. 

We did lots of fun things together with our housemates – impromptu activities like yoga / meditation / dancing / watching movies, as well as a regular check-in to keep up on each other’s lives. We were generally more easily exposed to new things – meeting friends of friends, trying new foods or activities that someone in the house liked, etc. Our friends often enjoyed playing with the kids, and it was helpful to have someone entertain them while we left the living room for a few minutes. Our 3 year old seems more social than most kids of the pandemic generation, which is partly temperament and partly growing up in a group house.

Cons. The main issue was that the group house location was obviously not chosen with school catchment areas or kid-friendly neighbourhoods in mind. The other downsides of living there with kids were insufficient space, lifestyle differences, and extra logistics (all of which increased when we had a second kid).

Our family was taking up more and more of the common space – the living room doubled as a play room and a nursery, so it was a bit cramped. With 4 of us (plus visiting grandparents) and 4 other housemates in the house, the capacity of the house was maxed out (particularly the fridge, which became a realm of mystery and chaos). I am generally sensitive to clutter, and having the house full of our stuff and other people’s stuff was a bit much, while only dealing with our own things and mess is more manageable.

Another factor was a mismatch in lifestyles and timings with our housemates, who tended to have later schedules. They often got home and started socializing or heading out to evening events when we already finished dinner and it was time to put the kids to bed, which was FOMO-inducing at times. Daniel enjoyed evening gatherings like the house check-in, but often became overstimulated and was difficult to put to bed afterwards. The time when we went to sleep in the evening was also a time when people wanted to watch movies on the projector, and it made me sad to keep asking them not to. 

There were also more logistics involved with running a group house, like managing shared expenses and objects, coordinating chores and housemate turnover. Even with regular decluttering, there was a lot of stuff at the house that didn’t belong to anyone in particular (e.g. before leaving I cleared the shoe rack of 9 pairs of shoes that turned out to be abandoned by previous occupants of the house). With two kids, we have more of our own logistics to deal with, so reducing other logistics was helpful.

Final thoughts. We are thankful to our housemates, current and former, for all the great times we had over the years and the wonderful community we built together. Visiting the house after moving out, it was nice to see the living room decked out with pretty decorations and potted plants and not overflowing with kid stuff – it reminded me of what the house was like when we first started it. Without the constraints of children living at the house, I hope to see Deep End return to its former self as a social place with more events and gatherings, and we will certainly be back to visit often.

It is a big change to live on our own after all these years. We moved near a few other friends with kids, which will be fun too. We are enjoying our own space right now, though we are not set on living by ourselves indefinitely. We might want to live with others again in the future, but probably with 1-2 close friends rather than in a big group house.

2023 review

Life updates

We received a special gift for New Year’s – Michael (“Misha”) arrived just in time to be born in 2023! Daniel is already getting the hang of rocking his brother and singing him lullabies.

Work

Last year I mostly focused on threat models for AI risk. This year my work was split between projects aiming to address to different aspects of our main threat model: dangerous capability evaluations, mentoring MATS scholars on understanding agency and power-seeking in language models, and internal outreach about AI alignment. In retrospect I was spread a bit too thin, and didn’t make as much progress on the evaluations project as I would like, since outreach and mentoring usually seemed more urgent. So I will try to be more focused next year. 

Research

  • Paper: Power-seeking can be probable and predictive for trained agents, investigating how the training process affects power-seeking incentives and showing that they are still likely to hold for trained RL agents under some simplifying assumptions.
  • Mentoring a research group on understanding agency and power-seeking in language models for the ML Alignment & Theory Scholars program. Out of 60 people who applied to the group, I supervised 11 scholars in the initial training phase of the program, and continued working with 5 of them (on two projects) in the main program.
    • One team of my scholars made some progress on understanding the limitations of agents simulated by predictive models (paper).
    • The other team of scholars performed a theoretical investigation of how well shutdown obedience is preserved when the environment changes slightly (paper).
  • Blog post: Some high-level thoughts on the DeepMind alignment team’s strategy
  • Dangerous capability evaluations (focused on persuasion and situational awareness capabilities).

Outreach

  • Created an internal Google course on AI alignment with Rohin Shah, attended by 600+ people in live sessions and made into a self-study course.
  • Gave an updated version of the Paradigms of AI alignment talk in various venues, including Cohere for AI, EAG London and the BAAI conference in China.
  • Spoke on the Inside View podcast about paradigms and threat models in AI alignment.
  • Did an interview with AI impacts on the strength of evidence for AI risk claims.
  • Updated the list of specification gaming examples to have more structured and detailed information about each example, with separate columns for intended goal, behavior, and misspecified goal. 
  • Wrote well-received blog posts on near-term motivation for AI alignment and why discussions of AI risks should talk about capabilities rather than intelligence. 

Health

Physical health. This year I got sick less often than last year (similar number of colds but no other illnesses). The colds also lasted for less long – possibly due to copious use of the “dual defense” nasal spray, and also because we were past the initial barrage of germs from Daniel starting nursery (though he still had a runny nose most of the time).

Mental health. Generally better this year. There were fewer episodes of particularly bad mental states compared to the previous two years, though still not at the pre-parenting baseline. Looking over my bug reports, I found that bad mental episodes are strongly associated with traveling with Daniel. Maybe it’s a good thing we probably won’t be traveling as much now that we have two kids.

After Daniel was born, I had recurring night terrors (being woken up by worries about the baby and looking for him in random places). Thankfully these have stopped at this point. Hopefully this was a first-time-parent-anxiety thing and won’t happen as much with the second baby…

In spring, I took Irene Lyon’s self-therapy course based on somatic experiencing practice, which involves a lot of “neurosensory” exercises where you pay attention to your body and perceptions in different ways. I found the exercises more helpful for my wellbeing than my previous meditation practice, so I mostly do these in place of meditation now.

I didn’t do as much meditation as intended, somewhat less than in previous years (likely due to travel). Unsurprisingly, I found that I meditate less often on Saturdays, which are the days we don’t have childcare.

Sleep. Average sleep was pretty similar to last year (7 hours a night), though there was more insomnia (23% of nights). This is probably because I was going to sleep earlier and waking up at the same time. (As usual, all the sleep metrics are excluding jetlag.)

Pregnancy. Overall I felt pretty well, though had somewhat more symptoms than the first time (some backache, sciatica, rib pain, etc). Had a bit of nausea in the first trimester, which I found I could keep at bay by continually snacking (thank you, office microkitchens). I also had some food aversions that for some mysterious reason were only triggered by the office cafeteria (maybe the sauces they use) so I stuck to plain food there.

Thankfully I didn’t have fatigue and was able to stay active until the end. My usual exercise routine of prenatal yoga and personal training once a week worked pretty well (for mental wellbeing and reducing various muscle pains). I continued riding my bike (on flat ground or a slight incline), which was actually more comfortable than walking since it didn’t give me backache. I found that exercise got easier in the last few weeks before birth, since the baby moved downwards and got his feet out of my lungs.

I had some issues with an iron deficiency that was not diagnosed right away. I was pretty tired during the Newfoundland hiking trip in June, got a blood test upon returning home and was recommended to take 100mg of iron a day (for reference, a typical women’s multivitamin contains around 15mg of iron). My next blood test in September showed that my iron levels were still going down, so I was told to take 400mg of iron a day (luckily I don’t get side effects from this). I wasn’t physically tired this time, but often felt unmotivated and spacey, which magically disappeared once I quadrupled the iron dose (now I know that iron deficiency can feel like burnout). These episodes of iron deficiency were bad for productivity and generally feeling like myself, which could have probably been avoided by more frequent testing and taking a multivitamin from the beginning.

Comparing this pregnancy to the first one (in 2020), I had somewhat better sleep and less insomnia for some reason – possibly exercise, since the first time was during the pandemic, so I was more sedentary. (Hours awake at night is not a good comparison point since it’s confounded by Daniel waking up.)

Parenting 

Potty training. This year, Daniel got better at using the potty with less prompting and more reliably communicating when he needs to go. During our travels, we didn’t bring a potty and used a kids toilet seat instead, but at home he preferred the potty. After we got back from Canada in August, we put the potty away and continued using the toilet by default – he complained a bit but seemed to get used to it. At some point he rejected the kids toilet seat and used the toilet without it (with a toddler stool). Once he entered the “oppositional” phase of toddlerhood, asking him directly whether he needs the toilet would always get a “no”. I found it was much more effective to say that I’m going to the toilet, and then he would say “no, Daniel is going to the toilet!”.

Since Daniel was staying dry at night some of the time, we made a few attempts to ditch the night diapers this year – once in April when he was 2.5, once in July, and once in October when he was almost 3. The last time worked much better, and he seemed to better understand what’s going on, e.g. talking about how we don’t pee in the bed. He’s been out of night diapers since late October with 5 pee accidents, so I think we can declare victory on this one.

The timing was consistent with our potty training book (“Oh Crap”), which recommended night training around 3 years of age. I’m happy that we didn’t have to go through the full process described in the book, which involves waking up in the middle of the night and putting a sleepy child on the potty. This happened to be a convenient time to try, since I often woke up at night anyway due to insomnia. Daniel was also waking at night more often for some reason and coming to our bed, so it was easy to put him on the potty then. After a couple of weeks he refused to go on the potty at night and would just hold it until morning. 

Breastfeeding. A year ago I was still breastfeeding Daniel around twice a day and wasn’t sure what the endgame looked like. He rarely fed at night, though there was a spike in wakeups and night feeds in winter (maybe a 2-year sleep regression). A few months later we went down to one feed at bedtime – he would have a brief suck (probably out of habit) and then move on to reading his books, rather than falling asleep. During early pregnancy it became painful to breastfeed, so I decided to stop and told him the boob is empty (which was true). He asked for it a few more times and eventually stopped. Overall he breastfed until 2.5 years, though more like 2 years in terms of actually receiving milk. One consequence (or maybe correlation) of stopping breastfeeding was that he became a lot less interested in me and more interested in papa :).

Screen time. Daniel likes to watch videos of nursery songs and moving vehicles (trains or airplanes). We are not sure what is the right amount of video watching and generally try to limit it unless it’s useful in some way. Sometimes showing videos helps motivate him to get dressed / go to the potty / brush his teeth when he would otherwise refuse, which is pretty handy. It also helps get him out of tantrums when other things don’t work. At these times he often pushes us away, but his favorite video of a train coming out of a tunnel would catch his attention and calm him down enough to receive comfort from us. Overall the heuristic of “useful video-watching” has worked reasonably well.

Effectiveness

Lights. I continued using the Lights spreadsheet for tracking daily habits, which I started using in 2021. The set of habits changed slightly from last year, but overall has largely stabilized.

Here are the habits that I kept from last year:

  • Life tracking
  • Fill out lights
  • Make a list of intentions for the day
  • Ask myself what I want today
  • Meditation
  • Exercise (today or yesterday)
  • Leg & shoulder stretches
  • At least 2 hours of deep work (changed to 1 hour at some point)
  • Braindump / journaling
  • Reading (today or yesterday)
  • Negative visualization on making mistakes
  • Take supplements to avoid / mitigate colds (replaced with “use defense spray”)
  • Appreciate a thing I did today
  • Exchange appreciation with Janos
  • Go to bed by 11:30pm (changed to 11pm)

Habits from last year that I dropped:

  • Practice effective rest (breaks during the day where I pay attention to what I want). I often forgot to do this, possibly because it was not concrete enough, and simpler ways to take a break like naps or walks were more helpful.
  • Use eye drops (to address dryness from using contact lenses) – no longer needed.

I did about 64% of the Lights on an average week (down from 70% last year), probably because I wasn’t filling them out as reliably every day. I started feeling more self-conscious about filling them out at my desk at work for some reason, and it was harder to do at home where Daniel would try to take over my laptop (because watching airplane videos is clearly a higher priority).

Time tracking. This year I continued doing time tracking during work hours. In an average work week, I spent 30 hours on work activities (compared to 27 last year) and 8.5 hours on non-work activities (compared to 10 last year). The overall amount of research and reading went down somewhat in favour of outreach and comms (much of the comms was also outreach-related). The overall increase in work hours was likely due to some combination of less illness, less time spent on exercise, and adding another office night every other week.

Deep work. I tracked 248 hours of deep work this year, compared to 363 last year. This was due to the increased focus on outreach and shifting my research focus from conceptual / theory work to empirical work. Deep work seems to be less of a good metric for productivity on empirical projects like capability evaluations, since I didn’t count running experiments / debugging / iterating on prompts as deep work. In light of this, my original goal of 400 deep work hours for 2023 seems particularly unrealistic, since I never exceeded 400 deep work hours except for 2019.

Digital habits. The number of times I unlock my phone per day went down from 25-30 in the first half of the year to 20-25 in the second half (a bit lower than the average of 20-40 last year). Phone use is correlated with travel, so the decrease over the year is mostly explained by a lot of travel in Mar-June and August followed by no travel. I also use my phone less at work and more on weekends (likely because I use more navigation and videos for Daniel then). There is a dip in the middle of the week, probably corresponding to office nights.

Last year, a major focus of my research was developing a better understanding of threat models for AI risk. This post is looking back at some posts on threat models I (co)wrote in 2022 (based on my reviews of these posts for the LessWrong 2022 review).

I ran a survey on DeepMind alignment team opinions on the list of arguments for AGI ruin. I expect the overall agreement distribution probably still holds for the current GDM alignment team (or may have shifted somewhat in the direction of disagreement), though I haven’t rerun the survey so I don’t really know. Looking back at the “possible implications for our work” section, we are working on basically all of these things. 

Thoughts on some of the cruxes in the post based on developments in 2023:

  • Is global cooperation sufficiently difficult that AGI would need to deploy new powerful technology to make it work? – There has been a lot of progress on AGI governance and broad endorsement of the risks this year, so I feel somewhat more optimistic about global cooperation than a year ago.
  • Will we know how capable our models are? – The field has made some progress on designing concrete capability evaluations – how well they measure the properties we are interested in remains to be seen.
  • Will systems acquire the capability to be useful for alignment / cooperation before or after the capability to perform advanced deception? – At least so far, deception and manipulation capabilities seem to be lagging a bit behind usefulness for alignment (e.g. model-written evals / critiques, weak-to-strong generalization), but this could change in the future. 
  • Is consequentialism a powerful attractor? How hard will it be to avoid arbitrarily consequentialist systems? – Current SOTA LLMs seem surprisingly non-consequentialist for their level of capability. I still expect LLMs to be one of the safest paths to AGI in terms of avoiding arbitrarily consequentialist systems. 

In Clarifying AI X-risk, we presented a categorization of threat models and our consensus threat model, which posits some combination of specification gaming and goal misgeneralization leading to misaligned power-seeking, or “SG+GMG→MAPS”. I still endorse this categorization of threat models and the consensus threat model. I often refer people to this post and use the “SG + GMG → MAPS” framing in my alignment overview talks. I remain uncertain about the likelihood of the deceptive alignment part of the threat model (in particular the requisite level of goal-directedness) arising in the LLM paradigm, relative to other mechanisms for AI risk. 

In terms of adding new threat models to the categorization, the main one that comes to mind is Deep Deceptiveness, which I would summarize as “non-deceptiveness is anti-natural / hard to disentangle from general capabilities”. I would probably put this under “SG → MAPS”, assuming an irreducible kind of specification gaming where it’s very difficult (or impossible) to distinguish deceptiveness from non-deceptiveness (including through feedback on the model’s reasoning process). Though it could also be GMG where the “non-deceptiveness” concept is incoherent and thus very difficult to generalize well. 

Refining the Sharp Left Turn was an attempt to understand this threat model better (or at all) and make it a bit more concrete. I still endorse the breakdown of claims in this post.

The post could be improved by explicitly relating the claims to the “consensus” threat model summarized in Clarifying AI X-risk. Overall, SLT seems like a special case of this threat model, which makes a subset of the SLT claims: 

  • Claim 1 (capabilities generalize far) and Claim 3 (humans fail to intervene), but not Claims 1a/b (simultaneous / discontinuous generalization) or Claim 2 (alignment techniques stop working). 
  • It probably relies on some weaker version of Claim 2 (alignment techniques failing to apply to more powerful systems in some way) is needed for deceptive alignment to arise, e.g. if our interpretability techniques fail to detect deceptive reasoning. However, I expect that most ways this could happen would not be due to the alignment techniques being fundamentally inadequate for the capability transition to more powerful systems (the strong version of Claim 2 used in SLT).
